registry.name: Pathfinder review concerns
registry.scope_statement: The source of truth for PR review routing, impact analysis, and change risk classification. Detailed review guidance and contract history are joined into the same records rather than kept in a second registry.

change_classes.description: Public contracts, schemas, test contracts, payload shapes
Build scripts, CI workflows, release automation, Docker or packaging
Tests and fixtures without runtime behavior changes
Touches multiple classes or classifier is uncertain

classification_policy.fail_open_statement: Fail open when uncertain: classify as `mixed`.
classification_policy.suppression_prohibition_statement: Do not suppress review when the change touches workflows, release, publish, Docker, schemas, storage, telemetry, permissions, tokens, auth, or stateful external effects.

category_defaults.role: Authoring defaults. Each concern carries its own resolved values, and those are authoritative.

signal_policy.statement: Signal counting: a matching changed file path = 1 signal; a high-value semantic hit (core symbol, API, state key, or contract name) = 1 signal; repeated low-value hits in the same hunk = 1 signal total.
signal_policy.high_value_semantic_definition: core symbol, API, state key, or contract name

semantic_evidence_requirement.statement: Never activate concerns using paths alone when semantic evidence is absent, unless the concern is always-on.

conditions: a directory with multiple changed files maps weakly to no concern
repeated high-value symbols appear with no concern trigger
most meaningful hunks are covered only by always-on concerns
coverage_gap_policy.suppression_prohibition_statement: Coverage-gap detection is a disclosure mechanism, not a gate — do not suppress reviewers to avoid the gap.

rule_sources.enforced_syntax_statement: Direct F5 DOM-sink syntax is mechanically cataloged in `eslint.config.mjs`.

extraction_policy.bounded_loading_statement: Do not load the detail registry wholesale during a review. Extract only activated concerns.

contract_policy.definition: A contract anchor records the deliberately established contract of a capability: its owning module, its load-bearing invariants, and the PR or issue that established it.
contract_policy.scan_with_anchor: The conditional contract evolution scan checks new PRs for conformance against a recorded anchor.
contract_policy.scan_without_anchor: When no anchor exists the scan must reconstruct the implied contract from recent PR history, which is slower and weaker.
rules: Anchors are optional per concern — record one when a PR deliberately establishes or replaces a contract (a typed facade, reducer, schema, or lifecycle owner), in that same PR.
An anchor states invariants and ownership, not implementation detail. If the invariant is already captured in the concern's `purpose`, the anchor may simply point at it.
Anchors are evidence, not authority: a scan that finds the anchored contract incoherent should propose replacing it, not enforce it.
Name contracts after the domain, never the vendor — a telemetry contract, not a "Faro contract".

Add a concern routing row when a capability directory is created, not when its contract is finally written — the gate cannot see a concern's history until the row exists, and rows that arrive in the contract-establishing PR miss the fracture window they were meant to watch.

invariant_policy.definition: A named invariant is one load-bearing rule inside an anchored contract, given a stable name so a code comment or test name can cite it as ``see `<name>` `` instead of restating it.
invariant_policy.reading_rule: Read the same way as anchors — evidence, not authority.
invariant_policy.ownership_rule: A named invariant belongs to exactly one concern.
invariant_policy.naming_rule: Name the rule, never the code that happens to hold it today.

candidate_policy.definition: Pre-contract candidates are advisory architecture hypotheses, not anchors.
candidate_policy.promotion_rule: They cannot create a blocking conformance finding until an implementation PR establishes the owner and records the contract.

authoring_policy.coverage_gap_response: When coverage-gap detection repeatedly points at the same unowned area, first try expanding an adjacent concern before adding a new entry.
authoring_policy.stale_selector_rule: Remove stale selectors that cause noisy activation.

migration_discrepancies.summary: The routing policy forbids activating a conditional concern on paths alone, but eight subsystem rows carry minimum_signals 1 — a single path match reaches that threshold — and the PR-summary skill describes path-or-keyword matching. Phase 1 preserves every source fact and chooses no rule.

sources.statement: Never activate concerns using paths alone when semantic evidence is absent, unless the concern is always-on.
build-and-ci, cli-and-e2e-runner, ai-subsystem, go-backend, coda-terminal, mcp-authoring-server, cross-tab-controller, and completion-records carry minimum_signals 1.
Describes activation as matching trigger paths or trigger keywords.

candidate_readings: Conditional activation always requires at least one semantic hit, and minimum_signals then counts path plus deduplicated semantic signals.
A single path match satisfies a row whose minimum_signals is 1, as the numeric thresholds imply.
Paths or semantic selectors activate independently, as the PR-summary skill states.

disposition.rationale: Held open deliberately. The approved evolution plan reserves changes to what actually activates for the post-cutover alignment phase, so no phase through Phase 4 may settle this by changing routing, and the two readings that would resolve it both do exactly that. Phase 3 therefore preserves current behaviour: the CLI applies the prose rule from CONCERNS.md line 30, withholds every concern that reached its threshold on paths alone, and discloses this discrepancy with the withheld ids on every route. The conflict between line 30, the numeric minimum_signals convention, and the pr-summary skill's path-or-keyword description stays visible rather than normalised.
evidence: architecture/concerns/test/parity-routing.test.mjs: paths without semantic evidence are withheld rather than activated
architecture/concerns/test/migration-dispositions.test.mjs: the activation conflict stays unresolved and disclosed on every route

migration_discrepancies.summary: The go-backend semantic selector is written as an inline-code word followed by a bare word, so the legacy comma-and-backtick parser yields the malformed value "continue` token". The intended selector is either the Go keyword or the two-word phrase; Phase 1 records both readings instead of picking one.

sources.statement: The go-backend trigger_keywords cell contains an entry that is not fully quoted.
A lone leading or trailing backtick is stripped, so a mixed entry keeps an interior backtick.

disposition.rationale: Either reading changes routing: the selector matches both candidate values today, and collapsing it would add or remove real semantic hits. Phase 3's mandate is to prove equivalence rather than to change activation, so the ambiguity is held open and matched permissively. The source cell should be corrected when the Markdown is deleted and the registry becomes the only source.
evidence: architecture/concerns/test/parity-registry.test.mjs: the registry carries exactly one unresolved selector and it is the recorded one

migration_discrepancies.summary: The routing-defaults table shows subsystem minimum_signals 2 and cross-cutting 3, while eight subsystem rows use 1 and analytics-and-telemetry uses 2. The extractor already reads each row literally, so the registry keeps the per-concern resolved values and records the defaults as authoring defaults.

sources.statement: Routing defaults give subsystem 2 and cross-cutting 3 minimum signals.
Eight subsystem rows use 1 and analytics-and-telemetry uses 2.

disposition.rationale: The per-row values are authoritative and the defaults table is authoring guidance, which is what the legacy extractor and the CLI both already do. evidence: architecture/concerns/test/parity-registry.test.mjs: every routing row column matches the typed registry record

migration_discrepancies.summary: The legacy parser strips a lone leading or trailing backtick, so narrative entries that merely start or end with inline code lose that backtick and keep an interior one. The registry stores the unmangled source text and splits annotated paths into a path plus a locator, so Phase 3 parity must map these entries rather than assert byte equality against legacy packets.

sources.statement: Strips a leading or trailing backtick independently of whether the value is fully quoted.
Fifteen narrative entries and one annotated code path are mangled. One annotated document path is split into a path plus a locator without being mangled, so seventeen entries are affected in total.

disposition.rationale: The artifact is fully characterised. Replaying the legacy backtick strip over the CLI packets reproduces the Markdown extractor exactly for all 27 concerns in both views, leaving one entry the registry cannot round-trip because its source wrote a locator outside the code span. That entry is enumerated in the parity fixture, and the registry value is the correct one.
evidence: architecture/concerns/test/parity-extractor.test.mjs: every concern packet matches the Markdown extractor exactly under the legacy projection

migration_discrepancies.summary: Coverage-gap policy never says which tracked files belong to the universe it measures — generated files, assets, fixtures, history, vendored files, and directories excluded from the tier model are all unaddressed. Defining it is an audit decision, not a translation decision.

sources.statement: States the coverage-gap conditions and disclosure rule without defining the file universe.

migration_discrepancies.summary: Anchor and candidate evidence is human shorthand. Whether an arrow means a range, a lineage, or a supersession, and whether a trailing plus means an open series, has never been reviewed. The registry keeps the display text and the extracted pull-request numbers and marks the relation unreviewed.

sources.location: contract anchor and pre-contract candidate tables
sources.statement: Evidence values include arrow pairs and a trailing-plus open series.

disposition.rationale: No consumer reads the relation. The CLI exposes only the evidence display text and the extracted pull-request numbers, and the contract-evolution gate reconstructs history from Git rather than from the anchor. Assigning a meaning to the arrow is an architecture-audit question with no current dependant, so it stays recorded rather than guessed.

migration_discrepancies.summary: The `test_path` verification kind carries two value shapes that resolve differently. Of its 17 values, 8 are repo-rooted paths that resolve against the worktree, and 9 are bare test basenames that do not resolve without a search: BlockEditor.persistence.test.tsx, useBlockPersistence.test.ts, useBackendSaveFlow.test.ts, useJsonModeHandlers.test.ts, dodge-session.test.ts, FloatingPanel.dodge-session.test.tsx, useHighlightDodge.test.ts, sidebar-handoff-wiring.contract.test.ts, and resolve-safe-target-path.test.ts. All nine name real test files that exist under src/, so the gap is the missing directory prefix rather than a stale reference. Both shapes are faithful to the source cells, which say exactly these basenames, so Phase 1 preserves them verbatim under one kind; a Phase-2 consumer that resolves `test_path` as a repository path must either search by basename or carry a resolution step.

sources.location: verification cells for block-editor-authoring, floating-panel, and full-screen-sidebar-handoff
sources.statement: Names test files by bare basename, while other concerns name them by repo-rooted path.

disposition.rationale: Both shapes are faithful to the source cells, so narrowing them would break registry parity with the Markdown while it still exists. Phase 3 confirmed all 17 values resolve to exactly one tracked file, 8 by repository path and 9 by unique basename, so a consumer's resolution rule is a basename search and a guard now fails if any value stops resolving uniquely.
evidence: architecture/concerns/test/migration-dispositions.test.mjs: every test_path verification value resolves to exactly one tracked file

migration_discrepancies.summary: The reversibility concern's `output_policy.values` translates footnote 2 verbatim and lists three values. The live review contract permits a fourth, `unknown`, which footnote 2 does not list, so a Phase-2 consumer validating emitted findings against `output_policy.values` alone would reject an `unknown` verdict the current policy scripts accept. Phase 1 preserves footnote 2 rather than widening it, and records the narrowing here.

sources.statement: Declares the reversibility field as reversible | partially_reversible | irreversible_without_cleanup | unknown.
Builds REVERSIBILITIES with unknown included; line 17 then treats only partially_reversible and irreversible_without_cleanup as one-way doors.

disposition.rationale: Widening output_policy.values to include "unknown" now would diverge from footnote 2 while the Markdown is still the published source. The narrowing is pinned by a test instead, so the cutover cannot silently ship a policy that rejects a verdict the live review scripts already emit.
evidence: architecture/concerns/test/migration-dispositions.test.mjs: the reversibility output policy stays narrower than the live review contract

statements: The manifest's top level is deliberately open: `ManifestJsonObjectSchema` and `RepositoryEntrySchema` are loose, so an unknown top-level key is extension metadata that survives parsing and is forwarded verbatim into the package's repository entry, unvalidated — the consumer owns an extension key's shape, because nothing checks it. Known fields keep their existing validation and their explicit entry mapping, so fields that deliberately do not reach an entry (`id`, `schemaVersion`, `repository`, `language`) still do not. `build-repository` owns the forwarding: it refuses the entry fields it computes (`path` from the package directory, `title` from `content.json`) plus `__proto__`, from a set derived from the two schemas' shapes rather than hand-maintained, warns on each refusal, and reports the keys it forwards. Nested manifest objects (`author`, `targeting`, `testEnvironment`) and every guide and block schema stay strict — the openness is the manifest's top level only. Promoting a forwarded key to a named field is the migration path: the explicit mapping takes over and the key keeps appearing, now validated. Annotation ownership (`managed-by` / `source-package`, evidence #1504) is a separate unlanded hypothesis and is not contracted here.

statements: `pkg/plugin/auth/id_token.go` owns inbound caller-identity verification; `pkg/plugin/app_platform_identity.go` owns the single verdict every proxy route reads. Two properties, both required: the ID token's ES256 signature against the live key set of whichever authority issued it — the stack's own `/api/signing-keys/keys` self-hosted, auth-api on Grafana Cloud, both full verification and neither a weaker check. The chain ORDER is a contract property: the stack is asked FIRST because it is the authority for its own callers, and asking an unauthenticated in-cluster address ahead of it would let whatever answers that name decide who the caller is; auth-api is reached only where the stack publishes no matching key, which is the Cloud shape (`{"keys":null}`) — and its `namespace` claim bound by RAW equality to the server-derived namespace from the plugin context, never a request header and never the token's own claim. The signature alone does not identify a stack: auth-api's key set is cell-wide, so the binding is what refuses a genuine sibling-stack token. Raw equality means a claim of `*` is refused, deliberately diverging from authlib's `types.NamespaceMatches`. `Verify` takes the expected namespace as a parameter and enforces it internally, so a new call site cannot drop the binding. Failures are one `identityStatus`, so no route classifies a failure its own way: rejected (no acceptable token) is the only time-recoverable verdict and the only one that may take a retryable status; `identity-unverifiable` (nothing this stack supplies makes verification possible) and `signing-keys-unreachable` (no source answered at all) are standing conditions that must disarm rather than retry. A source that answers with a key set lacking the `kid` HAS answered — the normal Grafana Cloud shape — so that is a rejection, not an outage. A new status must be named in both `//exhaustive:enforce` switches. Not established: binding a token to its presenter — a copied, unexpired token replayed on the stack it was minted for still verifies, an accepted residual. `docs/design/BACKEND_PROXY_PATTERN.md` §3 states the boundary.

statements: `registerAuthoringTools` (`src/cli/mcp/tools/index.ts`) owns the tool catalog. Multi-verb CLI capabilities group into one resource tool carrying a kebab-case CLI-named `operation` plus an opaque, help-derived `opts` bag; append-only child members (`add-step`, `add-choice`) live on the same tool as operations. The CLI runners are the sole validator of **guide content**; a tool may validate its own **argument shape** — `validateCommandArgs` preflights `opts` against the exact interface `pathfinder_help` publishes (both rendered from the command's Zod schema), and mcp-native tools own explicit top-level Zod schemas. Placement and reparenting (`before`/`after`/`position`, `move-block`, `orphanChildren`) are deliberately withheld, and the withholding is declared where the tool binds the command rather than on the command itself — the CLI still offers all of them, and narrowing the agent procedure is this surface's decision. Withheld or unknown parameters are rejected (`UNSUPPORTED_PARAMETER`), never silently dropped. `pathfinder_help` is the discovery surface, and it is addressable only for commands an MCP tool has bound — a CLI command no tool dispatches reports `UNKNOWN_COMMAND` rather than publishing flags no tool accepts. Within a bound command, new CLI capability reaches agents without an adapter change unless a binding names runner fields.

statements: One mount-time path owns restoration; `useBackendSaveFlow` owns save/publish/unpublish orchestration; `useBlockPersistence` is narrowed to `clear`. The editor is a partial writer of a whole-object-replace resource: `saveGuide` layers the editor-owned `spec` fields over the spec last read, and all three writes carry `metadata.annotations` and `metadata.labels` through, so `spec.manifest` and upload-script provenance survive a save the editor did not author them in. Inheritance is scoped to the resource the editor's content came from, and backend tracking is what encodes that — so tracking is set only after a write lands, never before. Overwriting an unrelated resource on a name collision therefore keeps the `resourceVersion` guard but inherits nothing, and a failed overwrite stays untracked so the retry re-asks: inheriting there would render the new guide as the old one's path and stamp it with a provenance mark the upload script's ownership check trusts. The spec passthrough comes from the LIST snapshot, so the conflict check guards what is being replaced for as long as that snapshot stands; re-reading the resource at save time would defeat it outright. All three writes merge caller-supplied metadata over the snapshot's per field, so partial metadata cannot suppress the `resourceVersion` guard, and all three fail closed when the named resource is absent rather than replacing a spec they cannot see. Absence is confirmed against the server before refusing, by a probe that does not commit its result: a transient LIST failure resolves to an empty list rather than an error, so trusting the snapshot alone would make a guide permanently unsaveable — while committing the probe would clear a live error and store that empty list, hiding the guide-library entry that is the only way to recover. The editor is also a manifest PRODUCER, not only a preserver: `deriveManifest` stamps the fields the content determines — `type` when none was inherited, `repository` when minting a fresh manifest, and `additionalFields.stats` / `additionalFields.startingLocation` — and leaves every other manifest field exactly as read, so an editor-authored guide is a complete package while a path cover page keeps its `type` and `milestones`. Stats are stamped only for a plain `guide`, checked positively so an unrecognised type yields no stamp rather than a wrong one, and an inherited rollup is never replaced with cover-page counts. `startingLocation` is owned CONDITIONALLY, decided per save from provenance rather than from the value: the editor writes or clears it only when there is nothing inherited to lose, or when the inherited value is exactly what the derivation produces from the blocks read alongside that manifest. That is what lets an author who deletes the `on-page:` requirement clear the prompt with it, while an uploaded package's independently authored value survives a title-only edit instead of being erased — the two failure modes pull opposite ways and only provenance separates them. A value that diverges stays the external author's; reclaiming it belongs to an explicit manifest control, not a silent overwrite. Derivation traverses in the same order as `walkBlocks` in the cross-block lint, and "first executable block" means the same thing in both, so the manifest cannot disagree with the entry-location advice `firstStepMissingOnPage` gave the author — including accepting a first-step `formfill`'s declaration, which the lint accepts and the editor itself suggests. The stamp goes under `additionalFields` because the CRD's `#Manifest` declares eight keys and prunes the rest with a 201 and a `Warning:` header `getBackendSrv()` never surfaces — so the invariant that the derivation introduces no undeclared top-level key is a test, not a comment. Fracture: #1599, #1600. Invariants in `purpose`.

statements: `runDataCheckQuery` (`src/lib/datasource/run-data-check-query.ts`) is the sole owner of query execution and its cost caps (15s abort, 100-point cap where the query type honours it, default 1h range). `useDataCheck` owns the check lifecycle and its `AbortController`. A check runs on user action only — including an engine-driven click, which the interactive engine can dispatch document-wide — never on a polling cadence, and only against a data source the picker currently offers. On an advisory check an authored `defaultValue` can seed that pick, so there "offered" is the guarantee rather than "the user chose it"; on a blocking one the schema rejects `defaultValue`, so a gating check only ever runs against a data source the user chose. A verdict and any completion it earned belong to that data source, and are retracted whenever the resolved pick changes, whichever writer changed it. A query that ran and found nothing (`'no-data'`) and one that could not run (`'error'`) are distinct states, and the author's failure message speaks only for the first. Abandoning a check aborts it, and an aborted check reports no outcome and completes nothing. `dataCheckQuery` alone enables the check; `dataCheckBlocking` alone decides whether a failure gates a section, and is the only shape under which an `input` block becomes a tracked step. guidance.purpose: Keep durable completion honest end to end: one emission boundary per terminal completion, one identity — the verified ID-token `sub`, never the outbound on-behalf-of credential — one record name (`hash(userID ‖ idempotencyKey)`) so a retried POST dedupes rather than minting a second record, one bounded queue that retains records an environment cannot accept yet instead of dropping them, and one denominator (`src/lib/guide-stats`) that publishes the block count and the per-block positions together so a numerator and a denominator can never come from two traversals.

statements: The Go write proxy (`pkg/plugin/completion_records_write.go`) owns the durable-write contract; `docs/design/BACKEND_PROXY_PATTERN.md` §11 states it. `deriveCompletionUserID` is the single identity contract — the verified ID-token `sub` verbatim — and both the read join key and the write's stamped `spec.userId` derive from it, never from the outbound on-behalf-of credential. The record name is `hash(userID ‖ idempotencyKey)`, so a retried POST targets the same object (409 is idempotent success) and two users' identical keys cannot collide. The response status IS the client's retry taxonomy: 401/408/429/5xx/3xx are transient and retried; 403 and 404 disarm writes for the session while RETAINING queued records for a later drain; other 4xx are terminal and dropped. The 404 disarm has three triggers — an upstream 404, `obo-unavailable`, and `identity-unverifiable` (a stack with no app URL can never verify a token, so it must disarm rather than take the retried 401). A write stales the namespace read index rather than deleting it, so a failed post-write refresh still serves the warm index. Client conformance is #1434.

named_invariants.name: payload-boundary-normalization
named_invariants.invariant: Identifier and title fields are clamped to the backend's byte bounds, with control characters stripped, at emission into the queue — not at send. A fact whose identifiers are still invalid after normalization is rejected before it is queued rather than occupying the bounded queue until a terminal 400. The backend stays authoritative; this only spares the queue and surfaces the drop.

named_invariants.name: disarmed-shared-queue-bound
named_invariants.invariant: The queue owns every unsent completion write, keyed per `(user, org)` owner. Its 100-item cap is per-tab and eventually-global, not strictly global: each tab enforces it against its own in-memory snapshot under a shared owner prefix, so N disarmed tabs can transiently persist ~N×100 keys until a drain reconciles. `localStorage` has no atomic multi-key transaction, so this is documented, not faked.

named_invariants.name: queue-eviction-concurrency
named_invariants.invariant: Draining holds a storage lease, renewed immediately before each send. A lease a tab persisted and that has since vanished means takeover-or-clear, so renewal fails and the drain halts rather than re-establishing one — that is what extends a progress reset's discard beyond the resetting tab, since `clear()` sweeps the owner prefix and with it the lease. The in-flight item is pinned so a concurrent at-capacity `enqueue` cannot evict it, and no outcome re-persists a record that left the queue mid-send. Each queued event's stable id is the required idempotency key, so a re-POST after a lease takeover dedupes to one durable record.

named_invariants.name: completion-write-latency-signal
named_invariants.invariant: Write health is reported through a typed outcome taxonomy — `created`, `transient`, `terminal`, `route-missing`, `forbidden` — surfaced as degradation reasons, not through a latency measurement. `route-missing` and `forbidden` disarm the session while retaining the records; `terminal` and past-retention records are dropped. Deliberately an exception to `TELEMETRY.md`'s measure-the-async-budget rule.

named_invariants.name: repository-identity-authority
named_invariants.invariant: Completion is keyed on `(repository, manifest.id)`, read off the resolved manifest and never off a loader URL. An explicit or resolved repository outranks any value embedded in the manifest, because the manifest schema defaults an absent repository to `interactive-tutorials` and that synthetic default would mis-key records. Only a _successful_ resolution supplies one: a failed resolution reports the last tier it probed, which is unconditionally `app-platform`, so its repository is negative-caching policy rather than an identity claim. The resolved repository travels end to end, emitter to record. A launch that carries no resolved package is not exempt: its loader synthesizes the manifest from the resource it fetched, so identity still comes off a manifest rather than off the scheme it was addressed by.

named_invariants.name: completion-denominator-authority
named_invariants.invariant: `src/lib/guide-stats` is the only place that computes the **stamped manifest denominator** or the **percentage recorded on a durable completion record**. The per-step model in `completion-store.ts` (and the path-level rollup in the learning-paths hook) is a deliberately separate model with its own numerator and is not in scope here — see `docs/developer/STEP_MODEL.md`; migrating it is a follow-on, not a rule this row enforces today. Within scope: the module publishes the denominator AND the per-block positions together, so a numerator and a denominator can never come from two different traversals. That pairing is per guide, via `computeGuideBlockIndex`; `rollUpGuideStats` publishes a path's or journey's totals only, so a consumer recording a percentage against a rolled-up `blockCount` still needs its positions from somewhere — the rollup index lands with the first path-level consumer. Containers (`section`, `assistant`, `collapsible`) contribute their contents and nothing of their own; `multistep`, `guided`, `conditional`, and `snippet-ref` count as one block each with their children outside the denominator. `snippet-ref` makes the stamped denominator the PRE-INLINING count, so a consumer indexes the pre-inlining tree; the splice in `inline-refs.ts` carries no provenance, so mapping an inlined block back to its ref is not available. Completable means "can emit completion evidence", which is narrower than "renders interactively" — `input` only in its blocking-datasource-check shape, `grot-guide` never — and `completion-affordance.parity.test.ts` holds that in step with the runtime tracked-step registry. Progress is the furthest position with evidence of completion — a "Do it" click or a "Mark as complete" click — and is monotonic, so reaching `n` counts `1..n-1` and preamble that emits no evidence is never individually completable. There is no completable-block special case: completion is `n / n` and nothing else, so a "Do it" yields 100% only when it is the guide's final counted block. `finalCompletablePosition === blockCount` is exactly that condition, and its negation is what makes a foot-of-guide "Mark as complete" button mandatory. `percent` reads 100 only when `complete`. A change to the counting RULE must bump `GUIDE_STATS_VERSION` even though no field shape moves — that stamped version is the only thing that lets a consumer tell an old-rule stamp from a new-rule one. On the CDN path the stamp stays at `manifest.stats`; on the App Platform path both writers — `upsert-learning-path.sh` and the block editor's `deriveManifest` — put it at `spec.manifest.additionalFields.stats`, because the CRD's `#Manifest` does not declare `stats` and prunes a top-level write silently. A reader therefore has two locations to handle. The editor stamps only a plain `guide`: a path's or journey's stats are a rollup over every milestone's blocks, which a cover page cannot see, so it leaves an inherited rollup alone rather than replacing it with cover-page counts. `manifest.stats` is declared at tier 0 (`types/guide-stats.schema.ts`) and reads as absent when malformed, so `build-stats` can still repair a stale stamp. That leniency is for readers only: `validate-package` re-checks the raw value and warns that the stamp is present and ignored, so a broken stamp never looks to an author like no stamp at all. Consumers ask this module for a position; they never derive one.

named_invariants.name: journey-threshold-membership
named_invariants.invariant: A journey completes on whole-set membership of its current milestones, never on a count. Comparing a stored completed-set's size against the milestone total lets stale slugs from a renamed or reordered path cross the threshold while current milestones are still outstanding.
